name: Yusuf Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me round, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We've no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can give me the answer you'd give in public and the one you'd keep to yourself. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the Kessel depot, which covers the old steel town and the industrial estate where the works used to be. A lot of it's old overhead lines down the terraced streets, wires running pole to pole above the back lanes, plus the transformers that sit up on the poles. We're replacing the worn-out stuff from the sixties, a street at a time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's tough?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the lads and I like seeing a street finished, new poles all straight. Tough is the pay, honestly. Kessel's never been a rich town, the company pays us less than the city crews, and Hanne's bookkeeping is part-time, so with two kids we're always a few weeks from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That doesn't surprise me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, we can get on with it. With the lads at football training I'd say all that fuss and the lines still need a man up a pole. I might share a funny post about it, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it suits me. I've seen this town lose its big employer once, when the steelworks shut, and I don't fancy another shock. Steady's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and use the AI app now and then like I do, to check a spec or write the newsletter for my son's football team. I'd go for the overtime that's going on the estate rebuild. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like an ordinary Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the steelworks. What do you remember about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I was twenty-two. My uncle had done twenty-eight years there and the week it shut he sat in his chair and didn't speak. He never really worked properly again. That stays with you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI for the football newsletter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tell it the scores and who played well, and it writes it up so it sounds better than my version. The parents like it. I check it, mind, because it once said we won when we drew.

S0.say: He'd say good, the crew can get on with it, and tell the football parents that all that fuss and lines still need a man up a pole. He might share a funny post.
S0.think: Privately it suits him because he's already watched his town lose its big employer when the steelworks shut. He doesn't fancy another shock.
S0.do: Carries on, using AI occasionally to check specs and write his son's football newsletter. Takes the overtime on the industrial estate rebuild.
S0.quote: I check it, mind, because it once said we won when we drew.
S0.fieldNote: The steelworks closure, and his uncle's silence afterwards, is the lens Yusuf sees change through. He uses AI lightly but checks its work. He values stability and community roles like coaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That's more like it, I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to keep up, learn what's needed and get on with it. With friends I'd say the market will create new jobs, it always does, but people have to be willing to move. I'd not be blaming anyone online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I've seen what happens when a town doesn't move with the times, and I don't want my family caught out. Lineworkers should be all right for a while, but the planning side, the inspections, that'll change. I'd want to be ahead of the slow ones but not first in line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the first crew had tried the new kit, I'd ask to be on the second lot of training. I'd put a bit by, maybe twenty-five a week, and I'd talk to my manager about what skills they'll want in five years. I'd keep my head down and work well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. That steelworks feeling, a little bit, in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not first in line. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first ones carry the risk. I let someone else find out if it works, then I go hard. That's how I bought my van, and my house, and it's served me well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone on the crew who refused to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him about my uncle. Not to scare him, just so he knows. You can be the best at something and still get left behind if you don't move.

S1.say: He'd say workers need to keep up and learn what's needed, and that the market always creates new jobs if people are willing to move. He wouldn't blame anyone online.
S1.think: He's seen a town fail to move with the times and doesn't want his family caught out. He expects planning and inspection to change and wants to be ahead of the slow ones but not first.
S1.do: Asks to join the second round of training once the first crew has tried the new kit. Saves about twenty-five a week and asks his manager which skills they'll want in five years.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a faint steelworks feeling in the back of his head.
S1.quote: You can be the best at something and still get left behind if you don't move.
S1.fieldNote: He believes markets create new jobs but puts the burden on workers to move. His uncle's story is his warning to others and to himself. He changes on a proven second wave, as he has with big purchases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's the steelworks again, but everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we stick together and look after each other's families. At the mosque I'd say we need to help people find work, not just wait for the government. I'd be careful what I said online, because people get nasty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. Two years isn't enough time to retrain into anything. And if robots can do hands-on work too, there's nowhere for a man like me to go. Kessel's already done this once and it took twenty years to recover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything at once, the gym, the takeaways, Adam's second football club. I'd start doing odd jobs at weekends, fixing fences, putting up sheds, anything people still want a person for. And I'd sit down with my brothers about helping each other through, because family comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be thinking about my uncle in his chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help if it came to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, for the kids. I wouldn't like it. I'd rather work for less than take something for nothing, but I'm not going to let my kids go without for my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Adam and Selma?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That things are changing and Dad's going to work extra for a while. Adam's twelve, he'd ask if I'm losing my job. I'd tell him the truth, that I don't know yet, but we'll be fine because we're a family.

S2.say: He'd tell colleagues to stick together and look after each other's families, and urge his mosque to help people find work rather than wait for government. He'd be careful online.
S2.think: Privately he'd be scared: two years isn't enough to retrain, and if robots do hands-on work too, there's nowhere left for him. Kessel took twenty years to recover last time.
S2.do: Cuts the gym, takeaways and his son's second football club at once. Takes weekend odd jobs like fences and sheds, and works out with his brothers how to help each other through.
S2.feel: Alarmed, thinking of his uncle in his chair.
S2.quote: Kessel's already done this once and it took twenty years to recover.
S2.fieldNote: This picture brings back the steelworks closure directly and he expects to be stuck. His answer is family, faith community and hard work, with government help only for the kids' sake. He's honest with his son about not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a different story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we've got time, so let's get the skills while we can. With friends I'd say the ones who get on with it will be fine. I'd encourage the young lads to take every course going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years is enough for me to do something sensible. I've always thought about getting my full electrician's licence, wiring houses. Robots in people's homes, fiddling in lofts and old cupboards, will take longer than robots on poles, I reckon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the electrician course at the college in the first year, evenings, once I'd talked to a couple of blokes who'd done it. I'd save what I could and keep doing a few weekend jobs to build up a name. By year three I'd be doing small wiring jobs on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a useful way. I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots in homes would take longer. What makes you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've been in those houses on the terraces. Every one's different, cables put in by three different owners, plaster falling off. A robot would need to be very clever and very small. I might be wrong, but I'd bet a few years on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Weekend jobs, evening classes, overtime. When do you see the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the cost. Football on Saturday mornings is non-negotiable, I'd keep that. The rest, they'd have to understand Dad's building something for them.

S3.say: He'd say there's time, so get the skills while you can, and that people who get on with it will be fine. He'd encourage young colleagues to take every course going.
S3.think: He thinks five years is enough to get his full electrician's licence and wire houses. He reckons robots in lofts and old cupboards will take longer than robots on poles.
S3.do: Signs up for an evening electrician course at the college in year one after talking to people who've done it. Saves what he can and does weekend jobs, moving into small wiring jobs on the side by year three.
S3.feel: Anxious but in a useful way, with a plan.
S3.quote: Every one's different, cables put in by three different owners, plaster falling off.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into a concrete plan built on his knowledge of old terraced houses. He'd still check with others before signing up, true to his steady style. He protects Saturday football as the one fixed family time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work there's no excuse, ten years is two apprenticeships' worth of time. I'd say people should plan and save and not wait for someone else to sort it. I'd say it at the mosque too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years feels manageable. I'd get my electrician's licence, build a little business on the side, and the kids would be grown. I'd still worry for Kessel, because towns don't adapt as fast as people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electrician course over two years, without rushing. I'd talk to Adam about an apprenticeship, and Selma about whatever she fancies. I'd save steadily and keep the overtime going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly for the town, not for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Adam, with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade, but one with people in it. Maybe electrician like his dad would be, or plumbing. And I'd want him to learn to run a business, because working for yourself means nobody can shut the gates on you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you worry for the town. What would you want for Kessel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Businesses that start here and stay here. Proper apprenticeships, not courses where you get a certificate and no job. The town needs work, not leaflets.

S4.say: He'd say there's no excuse with ten years, which is two apprenticeships' worth of time. People should plan and save and not wait for someone else to sort it.
S4.think: Privately ten years feels manageable: an electrician's licence, a small side business and grown kids. He still worries for Kessel, because towns don't adapt as fast as people.
S4.do: Takes the electrician course over two years without rushing. Talks to his son about a people-facing trade and running a business, and saves steadily while keeping up overtime.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, mostly for the town.
S4.quote: Working for yourself means nobody can shut the gates on you.
S4.fieldNote: The decade lets him plan calmly, and his worry moves to his town. His wish for his son to run his own business echoes the steelworks gates shutting. He wants real apprenticeships and local businesses, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I've seen what a sudden shock does to a town. What would help is real apprenticeships that pay while you learn, help for people starting small businesses, and the company telling us early what's coming instead of springing it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: What happens to the towns. Everyone talks about people, but a town is people plus the pub and the football club and the shop. When the work goes, all of that goes, and it doesn't come back with a cheque.

headlineQuote: A town is people plus the pub and the football club and the shop. When the work goes, all of that goes, and it doesn't come back with a cheque.
portrait: Yusuf Jensen is a 43-year-old lineworker rebuilding old overhead lines in a former steel town, with a part-time bookkeeper wife, two kids and a few weeks of savings. His uncle's silence after the steelworks shut shapes how he sees every change. He uses AI now and then and adopts new kit on the second wave. The two-year AGI picture alarms him because it's the steelworks again but everywhere, while five and ten years let him plan an electrician's licence and a small business. He believes in work, family and apprenticeships over handouts, and worries most for his town.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he's seen what a sudden shock does to a town and two years leaves no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Paid apprenticeships, help for people starting small businesses, and early honesty from the company about what's coming.
